entry.title: Combined summary - Lichen: L2s In CHannels ENforced on bitcoin
entry.summary: The proposal outlined by AdamISZ/waxwing presents a novel mechanism for handling tokens on a layer 2 (L2) network linked to Bitcoin without requiring trust in the hub's honesty or operational status. The system utilizes contracts between a single hub and users, enabling users to hold and withdraw hub’s tokens as Bitcoin. These L2 tokens are collateralized by Bitcoin within a user-hub multisignature output. In cases where a hub fails to process a withdrawal or is offline, enforcement is carried out on the Bitcoin network itself. This design does not necessitate any modifications to Bitcoin’s consensus protocol. Withdrawal processes utilize a programmatic statement that, when disputed, can be verified and resolved using BitVMX's on-chain search capabilities. The core technology involves a RISC-V program running a Groth16 verifier, with the proof of execution settled via BitVMX. This setup ensures that even if the hub goes offline, users can still retrieve their funds, although the hub must remain operational during normal circumstances to avoid disputes. Operational measurements on regtest have shown that this model can handle complex verifications efficiently, suggesting feasibility for real-world applications. However, the design also incorporates inherent risks and limitations, primarily surrounding liquidity and enforcement mechanisms. Liquidity issues arise because the hub may not always provide inbound liquidity, limiting a user’s ability to receive tokens unless negotiated separately. This could relegate some tokens to merely represent credit, which carries its own risks. Furthermore, enforcing the validity of zero-knowledge proofs (ZKP) on-chain can lead to numerous transactions in worst-case scenarios, potentially necessitating additional infrastructure like watchtowers for practical usability. Despite these challenges, the system offers enhanced functionalities such as high privacy transactions similar to those in Zcash and versatile smart contracting capabilities across different hubs. The design's reliance on BitVMX for dispute resolution underscores a pragmatic approach to leveraging existing technologies, though alternatives like BABE might offer interesting variations specifically for Lichen implementations. Finally, concerns were raised regarding the potential vulnerability of the Groth16 setup to quantum attacks, given the current advancements in quantum computing. The possibility that the common reference string (CRS) used in RISC Zero could be compromised by quantum technologies implies that under certain conditions, the integrity of fund security could be at risk, pointing to the need for cautious consideration before deploying such infrastructures widely in environments sensitive to quantum disruptions. Learn more about the detailed implementation and ongoing updates from [AdamISZ/waxwing's repository](https://github.com/AdamISZ/lichen/blob/master/papers/lichen-draft.pdf).
